one_liner: nginx-style edge server in pure Zig (HTTP/1.1, TLS 1.3, HTTP/3, proxy); beats nginx on fixed, proxied and TLS keep-alive rows.
what_it_does: routez is a standalone edge server, not a library: static files, reverse proxy with load balancing and health checks, TLS 1.3 termination, HTTP/3 and WebTransport, ACME certificates, layer-4 TCP/UDP proxies, rewrites, limit_req and access control. It copies nginx semantics (location matching order, root, try_files, rewrite flags, open_file_cache) but is configured with a Zig ZON file, so nginx.conf does not carry over. It runs with no C dependencies beyond libc; TLS and QUIC come from the author's quic-zig, built as a sibling checkout.
how_it_is_fast: Each worker thread runs its own libxev event loop (quic-zig selects libxev's epoll backend on Linux, the same readiness model nginx uses) on its own SO_REUSEPORT listener. Static files go through a per-worker open-file cache and, when the page cache holds the data (openat2 RESOLVE_CACHED, RWF_NOWAIT or mincore), are served inline on the worker; plain-HTTP bodies over 32 KiB use sendfile and layer-4 bulk traffic uses splice(2). TLS is quic-zig's sans-IO TLS 1.3 in Zig using hardware AES-128-GCM when built with -Dcpu=native(+aes+sha2). The README gives no profile that explains the fixed-response and TLS keep-alive wins.
when_to_use: Small-response or keep-alive HTTP/1.1 front ends where the author's rows show it ahead of nginx: fixed responses (627k vs 529k req/s) and proxying to a keep-alive upstream (262k vs 208k).
TLS 1.3 termination of keep-alive traffic with ECDSA or Ed25519 certificates: TLS fixed response 582k vs 324k and TLS 10 KB file 208k vs 152k in its table.
Many idle WebSocket tunnels where memory per connection matters (5.3 KB vs nginx 17.8 KB at 50k connections in its ws suite).
Experiments or study of a modern edge server whose benchmark harness gates response bodies and TLS parameters before measuring and publishes its losing rows.
when_not_to_use: Anything you need to ship or modify: the repo has no LICENSE file, so it is reference only.
RSA certificates, handshake-heavy traffic or TLS 1.2 clients: full RSA-2048 handshakes run 1.0k/s vs nginx 3.6k/s, ECDSA 7.1k vs HAProxy 8.8k, and TLS 1.2 is not supported.

HTTP/3 serving, on-the-fly gzip or large proxied responses: it trails on HTTP/3 10 KB (94k vs 247k) and 1 MB files, gzip through the proxy (5.5k vs HAProxy 15k) and 1 MB proxied responses (4.7k vs 7.5k).

Tail-latency-sensitive proxying or frequent reloads: held-rate proxied p99 4.30 ms vs HAProxy 1.79 ms, 27% vs 56% throughput kept under a connection storm, and 74 failed requests vs 0 with a reload every 2 s.
Production deployments generally: 6 stars, one author, and its TLS/QUIC dependency quic-zig says 'Not production-ready' in its README.

integration.form: standalone server executable built from source (zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast)
integration.dependencies: libc; endel/quic-zig as a sibling checkout referenced by path (MIT), which pins a fork of libxev (endel/libxev 8cc9850)
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll, SO_REUSEPORT spreads connections across workers); macOS builds on kqueue but does not spread connections across SO_REUSEPORT listeners, so extra workers do not help; on arm64 the build must detect AES or TLS falls back to software
integration.thread_safety: Not a library; worker threads each own an event loop, with a shared pool of file I/O threads (4 by default); upstream pools and health state are per worker.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — nginx-like semantics and directives, but a ZON config instead of nginx.conf, TLS 1.3 only, a backtracking-free PCRE subset (no backreferences or lookaround), gzip-only on-the-fly compression and HTTP-01-only ACME

gotchas: No license: the repo has no LICENSE file and GitHub shows none, so code cannot be copied; quic-zig, which it needs at build time, is MIT.

Benchmark caveats from the harness code: the bench.sh gate compares status and body only (headers are not compared, though routez does send Server and Date like nginx), and the held-rate suite (rate.sh, oha at half the slowest server's peak from a separate 4 s wrk pass) checks only for status 200. All rows come from Docker Desktop on an unnamed Apple M-series Mac, where the author saw 90% drift between separate runs, and the 10 KB static row reads 308k vs 312k (a tie) in the main table but '343k/s, 10% ahead' in the 'come off this list' table.

routez is built -Dcpu=native (native+aes+sha2 on arm64) while nginx and HAProxy are generic distribution packages; their OpenSSL 3.5 selects AES and SHA instructions at run time, so this mainly affects non-crypto code. Zig 0.16 builds inside VMs could miss AES entirely and run TLS about 10x slower.

The open-file cache is on by default: within valid_ms (1 s) a file edited in place is served with its old length and ETag, so a truncated file cuts the response short and a grown one omits the extra bytes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick routez over proxy-only claimants such as rproxy, Arc or Spire when you want static files, TLS, HTTP/3 and ACME in one process and a harness that gates identical bodies and TLS parameters and publishes its losses; the HttpArena entries (zeemo, zix, vanilla) are application servers with custom handlers, not nginx replacements. The missing license rules it out wherever code must be reused.
verified_claims_summary: First-party wrk runs (256 keep-alive connections, 3 workers per server, pinned cores, median of 3 x 10 s) on Docker Desktop on an Apple M-series Mac, 20 Sep 2026, routez 53d2011 built ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native with Zig 0.17.0 against nginx 1.30.5 and HAProxy 3.2.23 packages on OpenSSL 3.5: fixed response 627k vs nginx 529k (1.19x), keep-alive proxy 262k vs 208k (1.26x), TLS fixed response 582k vs 324k (1.8x), TLS 10 KB file 208k vs 152k (1.37x), resumed TLS new connections 17k vs 13k; the plain 10 KB static file is a tie and many other rows lose.
status_note: Actively developed (192 commits, last 2026-10-03) by one author with 6 stars and 0 forks; no license, so reference only, and it depends on quic-zig, which describes itself as not production-ready.
